experiment.title: Find the real buyer
experiment.hypothesis: Students both use and pay for dinner
experiment.audience: Three evening graduate students who recently bought dinner, including cases where someone else paid or approved the purchase
questions: Describe your most recent dinner purchase: when, where, what did you choose, and what alternatives did you reject?
Who used the dinner, who selected it, who paid, and who—if anyone—approved the purchase?
What was the actual price, payment method, and any budget or reimbursement constraint?
What caused you to choose or reject each alternative? Record observed behavior, not hypothetical willingness to pay.
measures: For each of the three interviews, record the recent purchase, user, selector, payer, approver, price, payment method, and rejected alternatives.
Record whether the student both used and paid for dinner; preserve exceptions where roles differ.
Record repeated role patterns, notable exceptions, and unclear answers separately.
experiment.decision_rule: After completing the three remaining interviews, treat the hypothesis as supported only for this small convenience sample if all three provide concrete recent examples in which the student both used and paid for dinner. If any participant reports a different payer or approver, revise the hypothesis to separate user, buyer, and approver roles. This is not market validation.
experiment.limitations: The plan has five interviews total: two are reported complete and three remain. These are founder-reported, fictional convenience interviews with evening students, so the sample is small, selected, and unable to generalize. The two existing reports indicate price mattered more than speed, but do not establish who pays or approves. Task completion is not business validation.
